questions.question: How does visible strata layering (color banding, grain size, fracture patterns) function as an economic map where players who understand stratigraphy can predict which resource-bearing rock types appear at which canyon depths?
questions.answer: Strata control extraction economics. Sedimentary layers near the top yield fossil fuels and limestone; metamorphic mid-layers host marble and slate; igneous basement rock contains ore veins and gemstones. A player who reads strata color and texture targets their mining depth precisely, avoiding wasted excavation in barren layers. This literacy reduces extraction cost — the right layer on the first dig versus five shafts in unproductive rock.

questions.question: Do the visible rock strata tell the geological story of this planet — ancient seas, volcanic epochs, impact events — written in layers the player can read at a glance?
questions.answer: Each stratum is a chapter in the planet's biography: sedimentary bands tell of ancient oceans, ash layers tell of eruptions, shock-metamorphic lines tell of impacts — the canyon wall is a library.

questions.question: Can the player distinguish different rock strata by color, texture, and layering pattern at a glance, supporting the educational goal of teaching geological identification?
questions.answer: Sedimentary = warm banded browns/oranges. Metamorphic = cool grays with foliation lines. Igneous = dark speckled with visible crystal grains. Color palette is distinct enough for pattern-matching.

questions.question: Are stratum layer parameters (color, thickness, order) authored at build time or can they be modified at runtime and need to persist?
questions.answer: Authored at build time. Strata layers are part of the terrain material and are deterministic from the seed. No save/load needed for strata visuals themselves.

questions.question: Does strata formation simulate real sedimentary processes (grain size sorting, cross-bedding, unconformities) or is it aesthetic layering informed by geology?
questions.answer: Aesthetic layering for visual readability, informed by real geology. Layer order follows actual deposition principles (older below, younger above) but individual layers do not simulate grain sorting or cross-bedding physics.
